attacks.claim: The 14-day grace period plus Sentry/logs 30-day retention and Postgres snapshots kept 35 days means personal data persists past the stated purge date; the plan claims 'Nothing else is kept' yet backups and logs hold user data for up to 35 days after purge-day deletion of live rows, and the 'deleted_accounts' table is only described for restore, not for the purged-account window.
attacks.evidence: "Postgres snapshots roll off after 35 days and are not edited." / "Application logs and Sentry error reports have 30-day retention" / "Kept: ... Nothing else is kept."

attacks.claim: The 'Keep my account' restore contradicts the purge-registry and processor deletion ordering: Amplitude/Customer.io/Zendesk/Stripe deletions run after the DB transaction commits, but the flow never says whether processor-side deletion is cancelled if the user restores during the retry window, nor whether data already sent to processors is recoverable.
attacks.evidence: "After the DB transaction commits: Amplitude: user deletion API." / "Logging in during the 14 days ... restores the account exactly as it was" (no statement about processor state after purge starts)

attacks.claim: Stripe subscription handling conflicts with the 'exactly as it was' restore promise and with the 14-day grace claim: a subscription set to cancel_at_period_end at confirm will end at period end, which may be before day 14, so the user's paid access is cut off during the grace period while the 'Keep my account' flow is described as a full restore.
attacks.evidence: "the subscription is set to `cancel_at_period_end`, so it never renews during the grace period. "Keep my account" unsets it."

attacks.claim: Purge is a single DB transaction across 23 tables, and processor calls retry for 7 days with the purge-failed ticket only going to the privacy lead; there is no stated alerting or handling for a partially failed Stripe/Apple revoke that leaves the Art. 17 deadline at risk, and the 21-day success target conflicts with the 14+7=21 worst case while the 'one month' claim assumes no delay before the 14-day clock starts.
attacks.evidence: "Each call retries with exponential backoff for up to 7 days" / "100% of purges complete within 21 days of confirmation"

attacks.claim: The claim that no other system holds user-level data rests on an inventory dated Sep 2026 and the plan names only five processors, yet the plan also notes Zendesk tickets, Sentry, logs, and a 'club messages' feature; no evidence shows the inventory covered all of these or the 2.1M-account scale.
attacks.evidence: "No other system holds user-level data beyond the processors below (data inventory DPI-2026, reviewed Sep 2026)."

attacks.claim: The plan does not address minors: sign-up requires 16+, but deletion and retention of data for users who were minors at collection, and the Apple/Google re-auth for age-gated data, are not covered; more importantly, the 'club messages' deletion from others' views and the retention of Zendesk tickets containing user messages are not reconciled with Art. 17 and Art. 19 notification duties.
attacks.evidence: "Sign-up requires users to be 16 or older" (context) / "Zendesk: end-user permanent deletion." with no mention of third-party recipients notification

attacks.claim: The 'Keep my account' restore covers only the 14-day window; the plan does not state whether restore is available after the purge job has started processing a given account batch, creating an ambiguous one-way door.
attacks.evidence: "Logging in during the 14 days shows ... 'Keep my account'"

attacks.claim: Screen 1 offers 'Download my data first' but the export is emailed as a ZIP while the account is deactivated; users who cannot log in via the web path may not receive an export link, and the plan does not say whether the export is available after deactivation.
attacks.evidence: "'Download my data first' links to the existing data export (emailed ZIP)."

attacks.claim: The purge registry CI test checks only columns in db/schema.rb, so tables referencing users through non-'user_id' names or join tables are not caught; the 23-table count is not verified against the registry.
attacks.evidence: "A CI test fails if any such column in `db/schema.rb` is missing from the registry"

attacks.claim: The email-only path treats clicking the emailed link as re-auth, so anyone with access to the mailbox can start deletion without a password. The abuse section only addresses stolen sessions, not mailbox compromise or a shared address.
attacks.evidence: Users who cannot log in use parlo.app/account/delete: we email a confirmation link to the account address, and clicking it counts as re-auth.

attacks.claim: The plan says nothing else holds user-level data, yet it lists logs and Sentry as retaining data for 30 days and does not say they are scrubbed or purged. Push providers (APNs/FCM device tokens) and any object storage are not mentioned, so erasure completeness cannot be confirmed.
attacks.evidence: No other system holds user-level data beyond the processors below ... Application logs and Sentry error reports have 30-day retention (privacy policy §7).

attacks.claim: Erasure depends on five external processors on the critical path, with no stated fallback, data residency for EU users, or exit plan if a vendor's deletion API changes or is unavailable.
attacks.evidence: Amplitude: user deletion API. Customer.io: DELETE /customers/{id}. Zendesk: end-user permanent deletion.

attacks.claim: Each account is one transaction across 23 tables, and the nightly job has no stated batch size, throughput, or lock-duration budget. At 100% rollout over 2.1M accounts, large nullify/delete transactions on hot tables could lock production tables or leave the job unable to clear the backlog.
attacks.evidence: each account is one DB transaction across `users` and the 23 tables that reference it.

attacks.claim: No cost estimate is given for processor API calls, retries over 7 days, or the Apple revoke calls at peak volume. Probably small, but unquantified.
attacks.evidence: Each call retries with exponential backoff for up to 7 days

attacks.claim: Alerting covers only processor failures (purge-failed ticket). If AccountPurgeJob itself stalls, crashes, or a per-account transaction fails repeatedly, nothing alerts. The one-month Art. 17 deadline is then missed silently, and the 21-day metric is only a dashboard.
attacks.evidence: anything still failing opens a `purge-failed` ticket for the privacy lead. ... A dashboard shows pending, completed and failed per processor.

attacks.claim: The registry CI test checks only that columns are present, not that each action is correct. A wrong 'delete' on rows owned by other users (club messages, friend relations, leaderboard entries) is irreversible after day 14 and is not caught by any gate beyond a manual dry-run check by one person.
attacks.evidence: A CI test fails if any such column in `db/schema.rb` is missing from the registry

attacks.claim: The restore runbook re-applies purges from deleted_accounts, but that table lives inside the same database that gets restored. Purges that happened after the snapshot time are absent from the restored table, so those accounts would be resurrected. The claim that a restore cannot resurrect a deleted account does not hold.
attacks.evidence: the restore runbook re-applies purges from it after any restore, so a restore cannot resurrect a deleted account.

attacks.claim: Sign in with Apple revocation runs after the DB transaction commits, but the refresh token is presumably stored on the users row that the transaction just deleted. Retries for up to 7 days then have no token to revoke. Where the token is captured before purge is not specified.
attacks.evidence: Sign in with Apple users: `POST /auth/revoke` for their refresh token. (after: After the DB transaction commits)

attacks.claim: Race between 'Keep my account' and the nightly purge is not addressed. A keep click during the purge transaction could leave a restored account partly purged or a purge applied to an account the user just reclaimed.
attacks.evidence: Keep my account, which restores the account exactly as it was ... The link is single-use, signed, valid until the purge.

attacks.claim: The claim that the worst case (14+7 days) meets the one-month Art. 17 deadline ignores backups (35 days, unedited) and the cases where the 7-day processor retry window starts later than the DB commit. The arithmetic is asserted, not shown against the full timeline.
attacks.evidence: Worst case (14 + 7 days) stays inside the one-month Art. 17 deadline.

attacks.claim: No visual or copy defect found in the text; the flow copy is consistent with the stated behaviour.
attacks.evidence: One button: "Continue".

attacks.claim: No value-related defect found; the plan addresses the App Store blocker and the support backlog directly.
attacks.evidence: iOS build 4.18 was rejected under App Store guideline 5.1.1(v)

attacks.claim: For store-subscribed users the flow adds an extra deep-link step to a platform page before the user can continue, which adds friction.
attacks.evidence: with a "Manage subscription" button deep-linking to the platform page, before "Continue".

attacks.claim: Section 2 claims accessibility testing was done, but the Tests list in section 6 has no accessibility test, so the claim lacks evidence in the plan.
attacks.evidence: flow tested with VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard-only web and Dynamic Type XXL / 200% font scale.

attacks.claim: Web subscriptions are set to cancel_at_period_end at confirm, but screen 1 shows a subscription notice only for store subscriptions and screen 3 shows nothing about web billing. This is a silent cancellation, against the no-dark-patterns constraint.
attacks.evidence: Subscription notice, only when relevant (§3).

attacks.claim: Snapshots are kept 35 days after purge and not edited, so personal data survives beyond the purge and the stated erasure timeline. The plan does not justify this under Art. 17 or disclose it in the erasure timeline.
attacks.evidence: Postgres snapshots roll off after 35 days and are not edited.

attacks.claim: Where retry state and the 7-day backoff schedule are persisted is not specified, so the retry design is hard to test or hand over.
attacks.evidence: Each call retries with exponential backoff for up to 7 days

attacks.claim: Store subscriptions keep billing after the account is purged, with no way to use the service. The plan only shows a notice and does not describe handling for that period.
attacks.evidence: Deleting your account does not cancel your App Store subscription

attacks.claim: Purge timeline is internally inconsistent with the 'no PII after purge' claim: Amplitude, Customer.io and Zendesk deletions run only after the DB commits and retry for up to 7 days, so user data persists in third-party processors for up to 21 days after confirmation while the plan's success measure accepts that window. Art. 17 'without undue delay' and the one-month limit are also measured from the request, not the purge.
attacks.evidence: "Each call retries with exponential backoff for up to 7 days" and "100% of purges complete within 21 days of confirmation"

attacks.claim: Backups are described as rolling off after 35 days and 'not edited', so deleted personal data survives in snapshots for up to 35 days after purge; the restore runbook re-applies purges but no retention or erasure guarantee is stated for that window, and the 'Worst case (14 + 7 days)' deadline math ignores backups entirely.
attacks.evidence: "Postgres snapshots roll off after 35 days and are not edited."

attacks.claim: Deletion is scheduled for 14 days after confirm, but the plan promises users that the purge is 'permanent' and the 14-day wait means the Art. 17 clock and the 21-day success measure disagree with the stated worst case (14+7=21 days, not 'inside one month' for backups or failures that escalate to the privacy lead, which has no SLA).
attacks.evidence: "Worst case (14 + 7 days) stays inside the one-month Art. 17 deadline."

attacks.claim: Single DB transaction across users plus 23 referencing tables, run nightly, with 'nullify' for rows owned by others, risks long locks and partial-failure ambiguity on large accounts; the plan does not address lock duration, batch size or what happens to club/friend data of other users (nullify vs delete for shared rows like club messages).
attacks.evidence: "each account is one DB transaction across `users` and the 23 tables that reference it."

attacks.claim: Unauthenticated web path lets anyone trigger deactivation of any account by address; the email link counts as re-auth, so anyone with mailbox access (or a forwarded/compromised inbox) can schedule deletion, and the 14-day cancel relies on that same mailbox. The 'stolen session alone cannot delete' claim does not cover email-only access.
attacks.evidence: "clicking it counts as re-auth"

attacks.claim: Age gate (16+) is stated as a sign-up constraint but the deletion flow and purge do not address data of minors or the parental/age verification interaction; more concretely, the privacy policy §7 and §147 AO invoice retention are asserted without showing the retention period or legal basis for 'billing name and country' being kept after account erasure, and the statement that nothing else is kept conflicts with Sentry/logs retained 30 days and Zendesk ticket history.
attacks.evidence: "Kept: invoice records (amount, date, VAT, billing name and country) ... Nothing else is kept."

attacks.claim: The 'no other system holds user-level data' claim is load-bearing for the whole purge but rests only on a data inventory reference; the registry, processor list and Zendesk/Amplitude/Customer.io deletion APIs are not verified in the artifact (e.g. Zendesk 'permanent deletion' and Amplitude user deletion availability and latency are assumed).
attacks.evidence: "No other system holds user-level data beyond the processors below (data inventory DPI-2026, reviewed Sep 2026)."

attacks.claim: Notifying the privacy lead only via 'purge-failed' tickets after 7 days of retries, with no alerting threshold, on-call owner or SLA, means a partial failure can silently breach the Art. 17 window; the dashboard is passive.
attacks.evidence: "anything still failing opens a `purge-failed` ticket for the privacy lead. ... A dashboard shows pending, completed and failed per processor."

attacks.claim: Rollback with the flag off still lets confirmed purges run on schedule, but the first live purge batch is gated only on a manual dry-run review by one person; no second approver and no halt switch for the purge job is specified, so an erroneous registry entry (nullify vs delete) could irreversibly delete data for many accounts.
attacks.evidence: "the privacy lead checks the account list and per-table row counts before it runs live." and "the purge job ignores the flag"

attacks.claim: Subscription handling for App Store/Google Play users only shows a notice and a deep link; it does not state that the user will be charged again or keep being billed, which is the core consequence.
attacks.evidence: "Deleting your account does not cancel your App Store subscription"

attacks.claim: Accessibility claims are listed as tested but no testing owner, pass criteria or WCAG contrast/motion requirement is specified for the countdown and email-based flows.
attacks.evidence: "flow tested with VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard-only web and Dynamic Type XXL / 200% font scale."

attacks.claim: The grace-period notice 'scheduled for deletion on {date}' has no timezone specification, which could show the wrong purge date to users near midnight.
attacks.evidence: "Your account is scheduled for deletion on {date}"

attacks.claim: Nightly purge of 1,140+ requests/month with per-account transactions across 23 tables and per-account external API calls is not sized; no batch limit or rate limit for processor APIs (Amplitude, Customer.io, Zendesk) is stated, so a backlog could hit vendor quotas.
attacks.evidence: "Nightly `AccountPurgeJob` processes accounts whose grace period has ended"

attacks.claim: The CI check only catches columns named `user_id` or `*_user_id`; tables that reference users through other names (e.g. owner, author, sender) would escape the registry guard.
attacks.evidence: "A CI test fails if any such column in `db/schema.rb` is missing from the registry"

attacks.claim: The 14-day grace period plus purge window is not justified against the 'no dark patterns' constraint, and the 'Keep my account' restore path is not shown to clear the scheduled deletion state from the processors already contacted (none occur before purge, so this is consistent, but the email cancel link is single-use while the request can be re-triggered, creating ambiguity).
attacks.evidence: "The link is single-use, signed, valid until the purge."
